items.title: How to Read the Monthly Jobs Report: Payrolls, Unemployment and Revisions Explained
items.body:
Every month, one number tends to dominate the financial headlines: the change in nonfarm payrolls. It is easy to treat it as a simple scorecard for the economy. In practice, the headline is only the starting point. A careful reader looks at several pieces of the report together, because each answers a different question about the labor market.

This guide walks through what the monthly employment report measures, where its limits are, and how to put the pieces together. It is general education, not investment or financial advice.

## Where the Numbers Come From

The monthly report published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) actually combines two separate surveys:

- **The establishment survey** (sometimes called the payroll survey) asks employers how many people are on their payrolls. It produces the headline job gain or loss, as well as average hourly earnings and hours worked.
- **The household survey** asks a sample of households about their work status. It produces the unemployment rate, the labor force participation rate and the employment-to-population ratio.

Because the two surveys use different methods and samples, they can send different signals in the same month. That is not necessarily a mistake. It is a reminder that every figure is an estimate with a margin of error.

## 1. The Headline Payroll Number

The payroll figure tells you how many jobs were added or lost across the economy, excluding farm work, private household work and a few other categories.

Some points of context help:

- **Single months are noisy.** The estimate carries a sampling error of roughly plus or minus 100,000 jobs or so at the 90 percent confidence level. A gain of 150,000 and a gain of 200,000 may not be meaningfully different.
- **The trend matters more than any one month.** Many analysts look at a three-month or six-month average to smooth out volatility.
- **The "right" number depends on the era.** The pace of job growth needed to keep the unemployment rate steady, sometimes called the breakeven rate, depends on labor force growth. When immigration, population aging or participation shifts, the breakeven pace shifts too. A figure that looked weak a few years ago may be adequate today, and vice versa.
- **Composition counts.** Broad-based gains across many industries are generally a healthier sign than growth concentrated in one or two sectors, such as health care and government.

## 2. Revisions to Earlier Months

Revisions are among the most overlooked parts of the report, and they can be among the most important.

Each month, the BLS updates its estimates for the two prior months as more survey responses arrive. Once a year, it also performs a larger "benchmark" revision that aligns the survey-based estimates with more complete tax-based employment records.

Why this matters:

- **A strong headline can be offset by downward revisions**, leaving the underlying trend weaker than the first impression suggested. The reverse can also happen.
- **Revisions often show turning points late.** When the economy is changing direction, early estimates can miss the shift, and later revisions fill in the picture.
- **The first print is a first draft.** Treat it as a preliminary reading rather than a final verdict.

A practical habit: when you read about a new report, check the net revision to the prior two months before deciding whether the data looks stronger or weaker than before.

## 3. The Unemployment Rate

The unemployment rate is the share of people in the labor force who are without a job and actively looking for work. It is a useful summary, but it has quirks.

- **Small moves can be noise.** A change of one or two tenths of a percentage point is often within the statistical margin and may reverse the following month.
- **Why the rate moved matters.** The rate can rise because people lose jobs, which is a negative sign. It can also rise because more people enter or re-enter the labor force and have not yet found work, which can be a more neutral or even positive sign.
- **It can fall for unhappy reasons.** If discouraged workers stop looking, they drop out of the labor force and the rate can decline without any improvement in hiring.

To understand which story is playing out, look beside the headline rate at the **labor force participation rate** and the **employment-to-population ratio** for prime-age workers (ages 25 to 54). These measures are less affected by population aging and give a clearer view of how many people in their peak working years are actually employed.

The BLS also publishes broader measures, including the **U-6 rate**, which adds people working part-time who want full-time work and those marginally attached to the labor force. A widening gap between U-6 and the headline rate can hint at slack that the headline hides.

## 4. Wage Growth

Average hourly earnings show how fast pay is rising, and they connect the jobs report to inflation and household budgets.

- **Look at the year-over-year change** for the broad trend and the monthly change for the latest momentum, while remembering that the monthly figure is volatile.
- **Compare wage growth with inflation.** If pay rises faster than prices, workers' purchasing power improves. If it lags, real incomes shrink.
- **Mind the composition effect.** If lower-paid workers are laid off, average wages can rise even though no one received a raise. The reverse can occur when many lower-paid workers are hired.
- **Consider other sources.** The BLS Employment Cost Index and the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker follow compensation in ways that are less sensitive to changes in who is employed.

Wages that grow much faster than productivity can add to inflation pressure. Wages that stall can signal a cooling labor market. Policymakers watch for both.

## 5. Other Details Worth a Glance

- **Average weekly hours.** Employers often trim hours before they cut jobs, so a drop in hours can be an early warning.
- **Diffusion index.** This shows the share of industries adding jobs. A higher share suggests broader strength.
- **Job openings, quits and layoffs.** The separate JOLTS report and weekly jobless claims offer timely cross-checks on hiring and firing.
- **Temporary help and goods-producing employment.** These sectors are sometimes seen as early indicators of changes in business activity.

## Why the Federal Reserve Cares

The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices. The jobs report speaks to both. Strong hiring and fast wage growth may argue for patience on interest rate cuts, or for firmer policy, if inflation is a concern. A rising unemployment rate, downward revisions and slowing wage growth may strengthen the case for easing.

Markets often react sharply to the headline, but policymakers say they look at a wide range of data over time. No single report decides the path of interest rates, and the Fed's judgment also draws on inflation readings, financial conditions and its own forecasts.

## A Simple Checklist for Reading the Report

1. **Headline payrolls:** How does the figure compare with the recent three-month average and with the breakeven pace?
2. **Revisions:** Were the prior two months revised up or down, and by how much?
3. **Unemployment rate:** Did it move because of layoffs, or because people entered or left the labor force?
4. **Participation and prime-age employment:** Are more people in their working years employed?
5. **Wages:** Is pay growth outpacing inflation, and could composition be distorting it?
6. **Breadth:** Are gains spread across industries or concentrated in a few?
7. **Hours and other signals:** Do they support or contradict the headline?

## The Bottom Line

The monthly jobs report is rich, imperfect and frequently revised. Treat the first headline as a snapshot, not a verdict. The most reliable insight comes from combining payroll trends, revisions, the unemployment rate and wage growth, then watching whether the pattern holds over several months. Looked at this way, the report becomes less a source of dramatic surprises and more a steady guide to how the labor market is evolving.

*This article is for general information and education only. It does not constitute investment, financial or economic advice. Data definitions and release practices are set by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and may change; consult official sources at bls.gov for the latest figures.*

items.title: Mortgage Rates and the 10-Year Yield: Why Home Loan Costs Don't Always Follow the Fed
items.body:
When the Federal Reserve changes interest rates, headlines often suggest that mortgage rates will move right along with it. In practice, that link is loose. Home loan costs tend to follow the bond market, and in particular the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note, far more closely than they follow the Fed's benchmark rate. Understanding why can help buyers and homeowners read the news with a clearer eye.

*This article is for general educational purposes only and is not financial, investment, or mortgage advice.*

## Two Different Rates, Two Different Jobs

The rate the Fed sets is the **federal funds rate**, the target for what banks charge one another for overnight loans. It is a very short-term rate. It influences credit cards, home equity lines of credit, and other variable-rate products fairly directly.

A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is a different kind of product. Lenders are committing money for decades, and most of those loans are bundled into **mortgage-backed securities (MBS)** that investors buy and sell. The price investors will pay for those securities determines the rate a lender can offer. That price is shaped by long-term expectations about inflation, growth, and interest rates, not just by what the Fed does this month.

## Why the 10-Year Treasury Is the Common Benchmark

Although a mortgage can last 30 years, many are paid off much sooner, because people move, refinance, or sell. As a result, the typical life of a mortgage is often described as roughly seven to ten years. That makes the 10-year Treasury yield a natural comparison point, and the two tend to rise and fall in the same general direction.

The 10-year yield is not set by any single institution. It reflects the combined judgment of millions of investors about the future. Key influences include:

- **Inflation expectations.** If investors expect prices to rise faster, they demand higher yields to protect the purchasing power of their money.
- **Economic growth.** Strong data can push yields up as investors expect firmer demand for credit and fewer rate cuts. Weak data can pull yields down as money moves toward the safety of Treasuries.
- **The expected path of Fed policy.** The market looks ahead. If investors already expect rate cuts, those expectations may be reflected in long-term yields before the Fed acts.
- **Term premium.** This is the extra compensation investors ask for the uncertainty of holding a long-term bond rather than rolling over short-term ones.
- **Supply and demand for Treasuries.** Government borrowing needs, auction results, and demand from domestic and foreign buyers can all move yields.
- **Global conditions.** Interest rates and investor sentiment abroad can influence U.S. yields through international capital flows.

## The Spread: The Gap That Matters

Mortgage rates do not equal the 10-year yield. They sit above it, and the difference is called the **mortgage spread**. Over many years the gap has often averaged somewhere around 1.5 to 2 percentage points, though it varies considerably.

The spread exists because a mortgage carries risks that a Treasury does not:

- **Prepayment risk.** Borrowers can refinance when rates fall, which returns money to investors just when reinvesting it is least attractive. Investors want compensation for that uncertainty.
- **Interest rate volatility.** When rates swing sharply, MBS become harder to value and investors demand more yield.
- **Credit and servicing costs.** Lenders must cover origination, servicing, and the possibility of default, even when many loans carry government backing or guarantees.
- **Investor demand for MBS.** If big buyers such as banks, the Fed, or other institutions step back, the spread can widen. If demand is strong, it can narrow.
- **Lender capacity and margins.** When lenders are swamped with applications, or are cautious about the market, the rates they quote can drift higher relative to what bond markets alone would imply.

This is why a drop in the 10-year yield does not always translate into an equal drop in mortgage rates, and why a wide spread can keep borrowing costs elevated even when Treasury yields ease.

## When Mortgage Rates and the Fed Move in Opposite Directions

The gap between Fed decisions and mortgage rates has been visible more than once. In late 2024, for example, the Fed began lowering its policy rate, yet mortgage rates and the 10-year yield rose for a stretch afterward. Markets had already priced in the cuts, and investors were reassessing inflation, growth, and government borrowing. The lesson is that the Fed's move was only one input, and often not the deciding one.

The reverse can also happen: mortgage rates can fall while the Fed holds steady, if inflation cools or growth slows enough to pull long-term yields lower.

## What It Means for Homebuyers This Winter

Winter is often a quieter season for the housing market, with fewer listings and fewer buyers in many areas. Some practical points to consider:

1. **Watch the 10-year yield, not just Fed headlines.** It gives an earlier and more direct read on where mortgage pricing may be heading, though it is never a perfect predictor.
2. **Focus on what you can control.** Credit score, down payment, debt-to-income ratio, and loan type all affect the rate you are offered. Even a modest improvement in a credit profile can change pricing.
3. **Compare several lenders.** Quotes for the same borrower on the same day can differ. Compare the annual percentage rate (APR) and the Loan Estimate form, not only the headline rate.
4. **Understand rate locks.** A lock protects you from rate changes for a set period, usually for a fee or with conditions. Ask what happens if rates fall after you lock, and whether a float-down option is available.
5. **Think in terms of the monthly payment you can sustain.** A rate you cannot comfortably afford is a risk regardless of where the market is heading. Include taxes, insurance, and maintenance in your budget.
6. **Consider the season.** Slower winter activity can sometimes give buyers more room to negotiate on price or closing costs, though conditions vary widely by location.

## What It Means for Refinancers

Refinancing replaces your current loan with a new one, and it comes with closing costs. Whether it makes sense depends on more than the rate alone.

- **Calculate the break-even point.** Divide the total closing costs by your monthly savings to estimate how many months it takes to recover the expense. If you may move before then, a refinance may not pay off.
- **Look at the full loan term.** Restarting a 30-year clock can lower your payment but increase the total interest paid over time.
- **Weigh the alternatives.** Some homeowners with low existing rates may be better off keeping them. Others may consider a shorter term, removing mortgage insurance, or a cash-out option, each with its own trade-offs.
- **Be cautious about trying to time the market.** Rates can reverse quickly. Many borrowers set a target in advance, such as the savings level that would make a refinance worthwhile, rather than waiting for a perfect low.

## The Bottom Line

The Fed influences the economy and shapes expectations, but mortgage rates are set in the bond market, where the 10-year Treasury yield and the mortgage spread do most of the work. Watching those two pieces helps explain why home loan costs sometimes stay high after a Fed cut, or ease without one. For buyers and refinancers, the most useful approach is to understand the forces involved, compare offers carefully, and make decisions based on personal finances rather than on a single day's headline.

*Mortgage terms, rates, and eligibility vary by lender and individual circumstances. Consider speaking with a licensed mortgage professional or financial advisor before making decisions.*

items.title: 2027 Employer Health Plans: Why Open Enrollment Often Means Higher Premiums and Bigger Deductibles
items.body:
As open enrollment season begins at many workplaces, a familiar pattern is showing up in benefits packets: the cost of coverage is rising, and more of that cost is landing on employees. Surveys from benefits consultants and industry groups have pointed to continued increases in medical and prescription drug spending, and many employers say they are adjusting plan designs to manage the bill.

This guide explains why premiums and deductibles tend to climb, what to compare when you review your options for 2027, and how to avoid common mistakes before your enrollment window closes.

> **Note:** This article is for general information only. It is not medical, tax, legal, or financial advice. Plan details vary widely, so always check your own employer's official materials.

## Why Costs Keep Rising

Several forces tend to push employer plan costs up at the same time:

- **Higher medical prices and use of care.** Hospital and provider costs, along with greater use of services, can raise what a plan pays out.
- **Prescription drug spending.** Specialty medications and newer, high-cost therapies are a growing share of claims for many plans.
- **Plan renewals and insurer pricing.** Insurers and stop-loss carriers reset rates each year, and employers that self-fund their plans carry the risk of large claims directly.
- **Cost-sharing shifts.** To hold down their own spending, employers may raise employee premium contributions, deductibles, copays, or out-of-pocket maximums, or they may narrow provider networks.

The result is that a plan that looked familiar last year may cost more or work differently this year, even if the plan name has not changed.

## What Changes You May See

Not every employer makes the same moves, but common adjustments include:

1. **Higher payroll deductions.** Your per-paycheck premium may rise, and the increase is often larger for family coverage.
2. **Bigger deductibles.** You may have to pay more out of pocket before the plan starts sharing costs.
3. **Higher out-of-pocket maximums.** This is the most you could pay in a plan year for covered, in-network care.
4. **Changes to drug coverage.** Look for tier changes, new prior-authorization rules, or different copays and coinsurance.
5. **Network changes.** A doctor or hospital you use may move in or out of the network.
6. **Fewer plan choices.** Some employers consolidate options or steer people toward high-deductible plans.

## What to Compare Side by Side

Do not judge a plan by the premium alone. Build a simple comparison for each option:

| What to check | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Per-paycheck premium | Your guaranteed yearly cost, whether or not you use care |
| Deductible (individual and family) | What you pay before most cost-sharing begins |
| Out-of-pocket maximum | Your worst-case spending for covered in-network care |
| Copays and coinsurance | What you pay for visits, tests, and procedures |
| Prescription tiers | Whether your regular medications are covered and at what cost |
| Network | Whether your doctors, specialists, and hospital are in-network |
| Employer HSA or HRA contribution | Free money that can offset a higher deductible |

A helpful exercise: estimate your total yearly cost for each plan in two scenarios. First, a **low-use year** (routine checkups and a few prescriptions). Second, a **high-use year** (a surgery, an emergency room visit, or a new ongoing treatment). Add the annual premiums to your likely out-of-pocket costs in each case. The cheapest premium is not always the cheapest plan overall.

## Understanding High-Deductible Plans and HSAs

Many employers are expanding high-deductible health plans (HDHPs). These typically have lower premiums but higher deductibles. If you are enrolled in a qualifying HDHP, you may be eligible to contribute to a **health savings account (HSA)**.

Key HSA features to know:

- **Tax advantages.** Contributions are generally pre-tax or tax-deductible, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. Review current IRS rules for details.
- **Contribution limits.** The IRS sets annual limits that adjust over time, with higher limits for family coverage and a catch-up amount for people age 55 and older. Check the IRS figures for 2027 before you set your contribution.
- **Portability.** The money is yours and stays with you if you change jobs.
- **Employer contributions.** Some employers add money to your HSA. This can meaningfully reduce the sting of a higher deductible, so compare it carefully.
- **Eligibility limits.** Having certain other coverage, such as some general-purpose flexible spending accounts or other health coverage, can affect your eligibility. Read the plan rules.

An HDHP with an HSA can work well for people who are generally healthy and can afford to fund the account. It can be harder for people who expect frequent care and may struggle to cover a large deductible up front.

## Other Accounts and Benefits Worth a Look

- **Flexible spending accounts (FSAs).** Health FSAs let you set aside pre-tax money, but they usually have "use it or lose it" limits with specific deadlines. Check how much can be carried over.
- **Dependent care FSAs.** These can help with eligible child or adult care costs.
- **Telehealth and virtual care.** Some plans offer low-cost or free virtual visits that can reduce out-of-pocket spending for minor issues.
- **Mental health coverage.** Compare copays, visit limits, and whether therapists you use are in-network.
- **Spouse and dependent rules.** Some employers add surcharges when a spouse has access to coverage elsewhere. Look for new surcharges or eligibility changes.

## Practical Steps Before the Deadline

1. **Mark the dates.** Open enrollment windows are short, and missing one can lock you into your current choices for a year, outside of qualifying life events.
2. **Read the summary of benefits and coverage.** Employers must provide standardized summaries that make plans easier to compare.
3. **Check your doctors and prescriptions.** Use the plan's provider directory and drug list, and confirm with your providers' offices when possible.
4. **Review last year's spending.** Your past claims and explanation-of-benefits statements are a useful guide to what you may need.
5. **Look at the whole picture.** Consider premiums, deductibles, HSA or FSA options, and employer contributions together.
6. **Ask for help.** Your HR or benefits team, plan portal, or benefits hotline can answer questions about the specifics.
7. **Think about alternatives.** If you have access to a spouse's plan or are eligible for other coverage, compare it with your own employer's options. Marketplace coverage may be an option in some situations, so review eligibility rules.
8. **Confirm your choices.** Save your confirmation and review your first paycheck to make sure the deductions match what you selected.

## The Bottom Line

Rising health care and drug costs are shaping the benefits offered at many workplaces, and employees are often asked to cover more of the expense through premiums and deductibles. The best response is to compare plans on total expected cost and fit with your health needs, not just the monthly premium. Taking an hour with your benefits materials now can help you avoid surprises later in the year.

*Because plan rules, tax limits, and eligibility requirements change, verify the details with your employer, your plan administrator, and official sources such as the IRS and Healthcare.gov before making decisions.*
